name: Bluish Grey
lede: Bluish Grey is a grey with a cast of blue, a name that has been in colour vocabularies since the first mineralogists' charts of the 1700s and that, on screen, is barely blue at all.

sections.title: A grey that hardly shows its blue
sections.body:
The swatch here is #9C9D9A, a medium grey whose chroma is only 1.7, so it is almost neutral [1]. It lies within a CIEDE2000 distance of 7.8 of the ISCC-NBS 1955 color called medium gray, and the nearest other systems give it close neighbors such as RAL's Signal Grey, 2.4 away, and Ridgway's Pale Purplish Grey, 2.3 away [1]. The 2010 xkcd survey's own bluish grey is #748B97, a clearly bluer and darker color [1].

The swatch is therefore a safe middle of the group, and not the best picture of the name. The historical bluish grey was a grey you could see the blue in, and the aged swatches that survive have muted anyway [2]. Compare it with [[grey]], which leans slightly blue as well, and with the warmer [[taupe]] and [[nickel]].

sections.title: Werner, Kirwan and Syme
sections.body:
The phrase is a product of the mineral trade. In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner built a list of colors to identify minerals, and later naturalists extended it up to 1821 [2]. Kirwan's 1794 list, with 83 colors, already has the name in the grey group, between lead grey and pearl grey [3].

In 1814 the Scottish painter Patrick Syme gave each term a painted swatch and an example from the animal, vegetable and mineral worlds, and in 1821 the list grew to 110 colors [2]. His Bluish Grey is number 14 among the whites, greys and blacks [4]. His example is the back and tail coverts of the wood pigeon, with limestone as the mineral, and it is defined as ash grey mixed with a little blue [4]. A modern edition adds the leaves of sea kale [4].

The name worked as an ingredient in other recipes. Syme's Pearl Grey is bluish grey with a little red, his Leek Green uses a little brown and bluish grey, and his Cochineal Red is lake red mixed with bluish grey [4][5]. Sowerby, whose separate system dates from 1809, also used compound names such as yellowish green and bluish grey, but naturalists found his terms too abstract [6].

sections.title: Older words for the same grey
sections.body:
English has many one-word names for a blue-tinted grey, and Paterson's dictionary lists a good number of them [7]. Latin *caesius* gives *caesious*, a bluey-grey bloom, and *griseous* means bluish-grey [7]. *Dove-grey* is the plumage of the dove, *Maltese* is simply given as a bluish grey, and *merle* is the grey-blue of a collie coat with black streaks [7]. *Mode* was a pale bluish grey that was a fashionable genre of light colors in the nineteenth century [7].

Others come from materials: *pewter*, *slate* and *battleship grey*, the last of which is how warships are painted [7]. [[slate-grey]] and [[battleship-grey]] are both articles here. *Berettino* is the bluish grey of the glaze used on Italian maiolica, and *mineral grey* is a bluish-grey pigment made from lapis lazuli [7]. *French grey* is a plain bluish grey in the dictionary's account [7].

sections.title: Mixing it
sections.body:
A painter makes bluish grey by cooling black with white and a touch of blue. Ball observes that Greek painters often used blue to darken, and that charcoal black stirred into white yields a clear bluish grey [8]. Rubens, he adds, was still making blues by this route two thousand years later [8].

The pigment trade has its own bluish grey. Blue lead, according to Toch as quoted in the Pigment Compendium, is not strictly blue but bluish grey, a condensed sulphate of lead tinted with carbon smoke [9]. Byzantine mosaic gives a different use: in one church dome the Pentecost scene shows red flames framed by white rays, and the rays are edged in a dark bluish grey [10].

sections.title: The grey of health and illness
sections.body:
Doctors and mystics have used the name too. Birren reports that the visionary Kilner took a bluish grey, tinged with yellow and red, as the color of a healthy aura [11]. In the same book's table of skin changes in illness, argyria, a staining by silver, leaves the skin bluish grey or slate colored [12]. In 1827 the Nuremberg dermatologist Heinrich Eichhorn proposed a bluish grey with yellow markings as one entry in his skin-color table [13].

These are not color names a modern clinic would use, and the aura claim is a belief and not a measurement. They do show how ordinary the phrase was as a descriptive tool.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, this bluish grey appears in 690, or 2.9 per cent, as photographed, and it covers enough of a canvas to count in 437 of them [14]. It is more common than 81 per cent of the named colors [14]. Inside a painting it is most often a light: 54 per cent of those 437 pictures use it that way, by lightness rank within each painting [14].

It peaks in the 1900s, when 54 of our 1,674 paintings, or 3.2 per cent, have it, 1.6 times the expected rate [14]. Its most devoted painter is Eugène Boudin, with it in 4 of 33 works here, 4.7 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [14]. [[painter:eugene-boudin|Boudin]] painted the skies and shores of Normandy, and the other devoted painter on the list is [[painter:gustave-caillebotte|Caillebotte]], with 4 of 22 works [14]. Norway stands out among countries, at 3.1 times the expected rate [14]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test.

The earliest hit is a painting of 1164, 657 years before the name's first record in our sources, Syme's 1821 list [14]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, and no evidence that the pigment existed. In printed English, *bluish grey*, in all its senses, peaks in the 1900s [15].

questions.q: True or false: Syme's Bluish Grey had a bird as its animal example.

openers: Syme's example of bluish grey was the back of a wood pigeon, with limestone as its mineral twin.
Look at the grey of a dove or of battleship paint: both are bluish greys, though few people would call them blue.
Bluish grey was already an ingredient: Syme used it in his recipes for cochineal red and leek green.
